title: Euler's disk
description: As Maya settles on flag 1, a hoop of red light a little wider than she is drops from the top of the column, lands on its edge on the glass around her and spins down like a coin settling: the wobble gets lower and faster, the whirr rises in pitch, and with a final glassy click it lies flat and tightens to the size of her taken ring at the column's foot. The column stays warm white throughout, and the hoop hands over to the game's own ring on the last frame.
twist: It borrows the most satisfying desk-toy motion there is. The speeding wobble is a built-in drumroll that everyone can hear coming to an end, and the end is exact: a click, and the ring is the thing the game keeps. On a flag other robots already hold, it settles on top of their rings, so the stack reads as a tally.
why: The most likely to get an "again!": faster wobble plus rising pitch is a tension and release everyone feels, it is pure light and glass with no gag to wear out over a game's worth of claims, and a spinning hoop of light reads from across the room even when the robot is small. About 1.5 s after the move, ending on the real taken ring.

title: Token flip
description: At the claim, the glass tile under the flag pops up out of the slab, leaving a square of darkness for a moment, and turns over once, all the way round, like a cardboard game token being flipped, with Maya stuck to it. Halfway through the turn she hangs upside down beneath the tile, seen through its smoked glass as if she had swapped places with her own reflection. The tile completes the turn and slaps back into the slab with a glassy clack: Maya upright on top facing east, her red ring now showing on its face, the column standing as it was.
twist: The oldest board-game gesture, flipping a token to its claimed side, done by the board itself in glass. For half a second the robot and her reflection trade places.
why: The gasp: nobody expects the floor to move, and a whole tile turning over is a big, clean silhouette that reads on a 12-space board. It takes under a second and stays on one square, so the rest of the board stays legible, and it is physical enough to stay satisfying the way a coin toss does.

title: Heads turn
description: At the claim every other robot on the board swings round at the same instant to stare at Maya, bodies, eyes and pointers all aimed at her. They hold for a beat, then all snap back to their own facings a little too fast, with a tiny guilty overshoot, like people caught staring. In the lab it is just Theo at (5,3); on a real board it is up to five robots at once.
twist: The robots have been rivals all game, and this is the first time they admit to watching each other. The joke is the snap back, and it gets funnier the more players there are.
why: A laugh of recognition: everyone on the sofa just turned to look at Maya's player too. Robots turning is the most readable motion the game has, it needs nothing new on screen, and the stare points every eye at whoever claimed. Every robot ends on its own facing, so the rules are untouched.

title: The detour
description: Maya lands on flag 1 and, far too eager, points straight at flag 2 and shoots off diagonally across the grid, a move no card allows. A space and a half out, the trail she is drawing goes taut behind her like an elastic band, a soft glass "nope" sounds, and it twangs her back onto flag 1, snapping her round to face east as her red ring drops into place at the column's foot.
twist: She breaks the rules in plain view and the rules undo it, which says "next: flag 2" better than any text. Lumen's trail, normally a mark that fades, turns out to be a leash.
why: Slapstick of character, impatience punished, and exactly the rule-breaking that snaps back into the rules that the brief asks for. A robot zipping off on a diagonal and getting yanked home is big, readable motion, and the direction changes every time (it always aims at that robot's own next flag), so the gag keeps teaching the race instead of just repeating.

title: Make a wish
description: As she settles, the column of light shrinks and flickers like a candle flame. Maya leans back and puffs (her eye flares and a little breath of light leaves her front), the flame bends away from her and goes out: for a beat flag 1 is a dark spot on the glass with a thin curl of smoke made of light rising from it. Then it relights warm white, with her red ring at its foot.
twist: Birthday-candle logic: the flag is a light, so the way to claim it is to blow it out. For a split second the flag seems gone for everyone, and it comes back because the others still need it.
why: The one made of darkness: where every other celebration gets brighter, this one goes out, and a tall column vanishing is the most visible thing that can happen on the board. Charm plus a small gasp, a ritual the room can say along with ("make a wish!"), and one the win can pay off later (the win list has trick candles).
